body_markdown:
We sometimes get fun member story submissions that[include a car](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/this-giulietta-spider-veloce-is-the-perfect-alfa-for-an-alfa-guy/) used as part of[a wedding ceremony](https://www.hagerty.com/media/hagerty-community/rides-from-the-readers-1959-triumph-tr3/) . They certainly do make[great accessories](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/saabs-connect-me-to-the-important-people-in-my-life/) on the day, and it’s entirely possible they could be “something old, something new, something borrowed, *or* something blue.” Talk about utility!


A few weeks ago, our own Andrew Newton tied the knot. Beyond how happy he looked—and how dapper he was in his custom suit—we all marveled at the car that starred in many of his wedding photos. Dude is cool. And it got us thinking: If we had it to do all over again, which car might we select as our getaway vehicle from the venue? Below are some of our choices; let us know in comments which car you and yours included on the big day—or the ride you wish you’d had.


## Grace, Space, and Pace


Juliana Jumper


This one is easy. We used a friend’s Jaguar Mk II for the big day, and I wouldn’t change a thing. It’s classy. It’s comfortable. It matched the vibe of the venue and event perfectly. I would also say it’s roomy, but, apparently, it wasn’t roomy enough for my wife’s ceremony dress (which she made herself, by the way!), so we just drove it about 50 yards from cocktails to the reception, after a change to dress #2. Totally unnecessary, but it still made for a nice entrance. — *Andrew Newton*


## Screaming Dove


General Motors


When my wife and I got married, we left the ceremony and didn’t go straight to the airport for our honeymoon, but we were airborne by morning, so it was close. Had we gone straight to LAX, I think our ideal car probably would have been a wagon of some sort. I’m not sure I could have pulled off a DB5 shooting brake, but I think a Pontiac Firebird Type K would have been a nice addition to our venue. — *Brandan Gillogly*


## A Caddy, but…


Eddy Eckart


My wife and I got married on August 31, which is about peak good weather in Northeast Ohio. Were we to have modified our schedule that day to require a motorized vehicle, being whisked away in the back of a 1967 Cadillac DeVille droptop would have been perfect.


This doesn’t directly answer the question, but I can’t ignore it: One car stands out from when I was courting my wife: a dark blue NC Miata. Early on when we were dating, my wife was in the process of moving back from San Francisco to Ohio, so I went out with her to explore the world she was about to leave. We rented the NC, and with our travel bags causing the trunk to bulge a bit, we hit the road. Down to the Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk and then up through the redwoods well north of Healdsburg, our week-long adventure sealed the deal for us, and that little Miata was there for every moment. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Triumphant Road-Tripper


Hagerty Marketplace/LBI-Limited


My wife and I got married in the middle of the Montana woods and then drove north into Alberta and over to Vancouver, B.C. for our honeymoon. We were in a Subaru Outback, which was … fine. But parked at the little motel where we stayed on the first night of our trip was a Triumph TR3. I knew *of* them but had never actually encountered one in the metal, and seeing it there before me, on such an occasion—it was easy to imagine just how fun it would be to drive with my bride across the Canadian Rockies, and then tootle around what is arguably the prettiest city in North America. In reality, somebody backed into the Subaru in a downtown parking garage, which mildly sucked but didn’t spoil the trip. I imagine I would have felt otherwise in a mint TR3. — *Stefan Lombard*


## Frantic Ferrari


Ferrari


When I was working on *Top Gear* magazine, one of the dumbest things we did was to buy a Ferrari 308 GT4 for Ford Mondeo money. Needless to say, the numerous repairs required of the Ferrari did not fit a Blue Oval budget, and the car was eventually sold for a loss. I did, however, borrow it to drive my sister to her central London wedding, and, after a jump start, it made it to the venue just fine. When my sister realized she’d forgotten her bouquet at my parents’ house I had to race back across town to collect it and get it the venue in time for the ceremony. Felt like a scene from a rom-com. — *Nik Berg*


## Big Finnin’


Thomas Klockau


Honestly, I don’t recall what we were driving at either of my weddings, but should another one happen, I think I’d find a very large, 1960s-vintage Cadillac with fins—the taller the better. It has just always been such an example of nearly achievable luxury and comfort and power. Might as well set a standard early on … that I’d likely fail to meet subsequently, if the past is any indication. — *Steven Cole Smith*


## Sorry About Your Hair…


Broad Arrow


Although I feel I had the perfect getaway car at my wedding, a Model A, it is fun to think about what kind of car might have been “better.”


A convertible would have been fun, since it was a beautiful summer day, and between the ceremony and reception my bride and I took a short cruise for photos and for some time to decompress and revel in the moment. And while she would probably protest, since she had her hair done perfectly, the fresh air would have opened up another sense to engrain the memory indelibly forever.


That said, a Mercedes-Benz 300SL Roadster would be my choice. Probably not hers, but[neither was the Model A](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/my-ford-model-a-nearly-ruined-my-wedding/) . She chose me, however, and the car came along too, whether it was desired or not. At least if we were in a 300SL, her dress wouldn’t have gotten oil-spotted… — *Kyle Smith*
